lessons.title: What a process is: PID, parent, /proc
lessons.goal:
Learn what a process is, how to see its identity, and how processes form a tree.

Why it matters: every command, service and container is a process. Troubleshooting a slow or stuck system starts with knowing which process is which and who started it.

setup.note: Programs are small C files (gcc needed). Numbers such as PIDs will differ on your machine.

steps.title: A program is a file, a process is a running instance
steps.text: `/bin/bash` is a **program**: bytes on disk. Each time it runs it becomes a **process** with a number, the **PID**. Your shell has one.

steps.title: Every process has a parent
steps.text: Each process records its parent's PID (**PPID**). `ps -o` selects the columns.

steps.title: The tree
steps.text: Processes form a tree. PID 1 is the first process the kernel starts (usually `systemd`). `pstree -p` draws a subtree. We start a subshell with two sleeping children.

steps.title: A directory per process in /proc
steps.text: The kernel exposes each process as `/proc/PID`. `status` has the name, state, IDs and memory use. `cmdline` is the argument list, `cwd` and `exe` are links.

run.output:
Name:	bash
State:	R (running)
Pid:	3461556
PPid:	3461434
Uid:	1000	1000	1000	1000
attr auxv cgroup clear_refs cmdline comm coredump_filter cpuset

steps.under: In the kernel, a process is a `task_struct`: a structure with the PID, state, a pointer to its memory map, its table of open files, credentials and more. `/proc/PID` files are generated from that structure when you read them.

steps.title: The first process
steps.text: PID 1 is special: orphaned processes are adopted by it, and the system stops if it dies.

run.output:
PID    PPID COMMAND
   1071       1 systemd-journal
   1094       1 systemd-udevd
   1446       1 rpcbind

quiz.q: What is the difference between a program and a process?
options: A program is a file; a process is a running instance of it
quiz.explain: The same program can run as many processes.

quiz.q: Which PID does the first user-space process have?
Where do you find a process's state and parent PID?

quiz.explain: `$$` is the PID of the shell.

check.scenario: You see a process `python app.py` using 100% CPU. Which two things do you check to learn who started it and what it is doing?
check.answer: Its parent: `ps -o pid,ppid,cmd -p PID` and then the parent's command; and its details under `/proc/PID` (`cwd`, `exe`, `cmdline`, open files in `/proc/PID/fd`). `strace -p PID` shows its system calls.

lessons.title: fork, exec and wait
lessons.goal:
Learn the three calls that create and run every process on Linux, by writing a tiny shell yourself.

Why it matters: this is what bash does for every command. The pattern explains PIDs, exit codes, why a child cannot change its parent, and why `cd` is a builtin.

setup.note: Programs are small C files (gcc needed). Numbers such as PIDs will differ on your machine.

steps.title: fork creates a copy
steps.text: `fork()` creates a new process that is a copy of the caller. It returns **twice**: in the child it returns 0, in the parent it returns the child's PID. `waitpid` makes the parent wait for the child and collect its exit code.

run.output:
parent: pid=3461604
child:  pid=3461605 parent=3461604
parent: child 3461605 exited with code 7

steps.title: exec replaces the program
steps.text: `exec` does not create a process. It **replaces** the running program in the same process with another one. The PID stays the same. If `exec` works, the old code never runs again.

run.output:
before exec: pid=3461613
after exec: pid=3461613

steps.title: Together: a mini shell
steps.text: fork, then exec in the child, then wait in the parent. This is the whole mechanism of running a command. `execvp` searches `PATH` like a shell.

run.output:
nosuchcommand: No such file or directory
[exit 127]

steps.after: The exit code of the child comes back through `waitpid`. A command that cannot be found makes `execvp` fail, so the child exits with 127: the same code bash reports.

steps.title: See it in strace
steps.text: We trace our mini shell. `clone` is the system call behind `fork`, `execve` loads the program, `wait4` collects the child.

run.output:
[exit 0]
3461635 execve("./mysh", ["./mysh", "true"], 0xffffd2c969b0 /* 55 vars */) = 0
3461635 clone(child_stack=NULL, flags=CLONE_CHILD_CLEARTID|CLONE_CHILD_SETTID|SIGCHLD, child_tidptr=
3461635 wait4(3461636,  <unfinished ...>
3461636 execve("/usr/local/bin/true", ["true"], 0xffffd5980cd0 /* 55 vars */) = -1 ENOENT (No such f
3461636 execve("/usr/local/sbin/true", ["true"], 0xffffd5980cd0 /* 55 vars */) = -1 ENOENT (No such 
3461636 execve("/usr/bin/true", ["true"], 0xffffd5980cd0 /* 55 vars */) = 0
3461636 exit_group(0)                   = ?
3461636 +++ exited with 0 +++
3461635 exit_group(0)                   = ?
3461635 +++ exited with 0 +++

steps.under: `fork` is cheap because the kernel does not copy memory: parent and child share the same physical pages, marked read-only. This is **copy-on-write** (next lesson). `exec` then discards that address space and builds a new one from the program file.

steps.title: Why a child cannot change its parent
steps.text: After `fork`, parent and child have separate address spaces, separate working directories and separate variables. Changing one does not change the other. This is why `cd` and `export` must be builtins.

quiz.q: What does `fork()` return in the child?
quiz.explain: 0 in the child, the child's PID in the parent.

quiz.q: What happens to the PID when a process calls `exec`?
quiz.explain: exec replaces the program, not the process.

quiz.q: Which call collects the child's exit code?
Why does `./mysh sh -c 'cd /usr'` not change your directory?
options: The child process has its own working directory
quiz.explain: A child cannot change its parent's state.

check.scenario: A script runs `cd /var/log` inside a `( ... )` group and then `pwd` outside it still shows the old directory. Explain using fork.
check.answer: `( ... )` runs the commands in a **subshell**: bash forks a child, and the child does the `cd`. The child's working directory changes, the parent's does not. When the child exits, the change is gone.

lessons.title: Copy-on-write: why fork is cheap
lessons.goal:
Measure copy-on-write: after `fork`, the child shares the parent's memory until one of them writes to a page.

Why it matters: it makes `fork` fast even for huge processes, and it explains memory numbers in `ps`, why a forked server may suddenly use more RAM, and how Redis or Postgres snapshots behave.

setup.note: Programs are small C files (gcc needed). Numbers such as PIDs will differ on your machine.

steps.title: A test program
steps.text:
The parent maps 64 MB and writes to every page, so all of it is really in RAM. Then it forks. The child either only **reads** one byte per page, or **writes** one byte per page. It reports how many **page faults** it took.

A page fault happens when the CPU accesses a page the page table does not allow (here: a read-only shared page that is written).

steps.title: Reading does not copy
steps.text: Reading shared pages needs no copy and no fault: the child's page table already points to the parent's pages.

steps.title: Writing copies the page
steps.text: The first write to a shared page causes a fault. The kernel allocates a new page, copies 4 KB (one page) and maps the copy for the writer only. One fault per page.
steps.under: At `fork` the kernel copies the **page tables** of the parent but not the pages. It marks every writable page read-only in both processes and keeps a reference count on each physical page. A write raises a fault; the handler sees that the page is shared (count above 1), allocates a new page, copies the data and gives the writer a private writable mapping. When only one process still references a page, it is made writable again without copying.

steps.title: Cost shows in memory accounting
steps.text: While parent and child share pages, each process's RSS counts them fully, so adding the numbers over-counts real memory. `Pss` (proportional set size) divides shared pages among the sharers. We start the program in `hold` mode: the child forks, touches nothing and waits 3 seconds. We read the **child's** memory summary.

run.output:
[1] 3461665
Rss:               65956 kB
Pss:               32836 kB
Pss_Dirty:         32832 kB
Pss_Anon:          32830 kB
Pss_File:              6 kB
Pss_Shmem:             0 kB
Shared_Dirty:      65608 kB
Private_Dirty:        28 kB

steps.after: The child has not written anything, yet its `Rss` includes the 64 MB it shares with the parent. `Shared_Dirty` is that shared part. `Pss_Anon` counts it **half** (two processes share it), so the real cost is about 32 MB per process, not 64 MB.

quiz.q: What happens right after fork to the parent's memory pages?
options: They are shared and marked read-only

quiz.q: When is a page actually copied?
options: When either process writes to it
quiz.explain: A write fault triggers the copy.

quiz.q: The child only read the 64 MB. How many page faults did it take (step 2)?
quiz.explain: Reads share the parent's pages without faults.

options: Divides shared pages among the processes sharing them

check.scenario: A Redis server with 20 GB data forks to write a snapshot, and memory use grows during the snapshot even though the snapshot code does not allocate. Why?
check.answer: The parent keeps serving writes. Each write to a page that the snapshot child still shares triggers copy-on-write, so the kernel allocates a private copy. With a write-heavy load many pages are copied and RAM use rises, up to nearly 2x in the worst case. Plan memory headroom and disable transparent huge pages (a write to one byte then copies 2 MB).

interview.q: What is the difference between a process and a program?
interview.a: A program is an executable file. A process is a running instance with a PID, memory, open files and credentials. See [the lesson](#/lesson/9/process-basics).

interview.q: How does a shell run a command?
interview.a: It calls `fork` to create a child, the child calls `exec` to load the program, and the shell calls `wait` to collect the exit status. See [fork, exec, wait](#/lesson/9/fork-exec-wait).
Twice: 0 in the child, the child's PID in the parent, -1 on failure.

interview.q: Does exec create a new process?
interview.a: No. It replaces the program in the existing process. The PID is unchanged.
Parent and child share physical pages after fork, read-only. A write triggers a page fault and the kernel copies that page for the writer. See [copy-on-write](#/lesson/9/copy-on-write).

interview.q: Why is fork fast even for a process with 50 GB of memory?
interview.a: It copies page tables, not pages. The cost is proportional to the mapped memory (page tables), not the data. Huge pages and vfork/posix_spawn make it cheaper still.

glossary.def: Process ID: the number that identifies a process.
The PID of a process's parent.
Creates a copy of the calling process. Implemented by the clone system call.
Replaces the program running in a process with another program (execve).
Collects the exit status of a child process.
Sharing pages after fork and copying one only when it is written.
A CPU exception when a memory access is not allowed by the page table; the kernel handles it (loads, copies or kills).
The kernel structure that represents a process or thread.
